courses.title: Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy
courses.description: Assessment and management of common musculoskeletal conditions: spine, peripheral joints, fractures, sports and soft-tissue injuries, and arthritis.

topics.title: Musculoskeletal Assessment
topics.summary: Subjective and objective examination, special tests, red flags and outcome measures.

material.heading: Subjective examination
material.body: The subjective assessment records the presenting complaint, body chart (area, nature and depth of symptoms), behaviour of symptoms over 24 hours (aggravating and easing factors, morning stiffness), history of present condition, past medical history, drug history, social and occupational history, and patient goals. Irritability (how easily symptoms are provoked and how long they take to settle) and severity guide how vigorously to examine. Red flags suggest serious pathology needing urgent referral: unexplained weight loss, history of cancer, fever, night pain unrelieved by rest, trauma in osteoporosis, saddle anaesthesia and bladder or bowel dysfunction (cauda equina syndrome), and progressive neurological deficit. Yellow flags are psychosocial factors (fear-avoidance, catastrophising, low mood) that predict chronicity.
keyPoints: Red flags: cancer, weight loss, cauda equina

material.heading: Objective examination
material.body: The objective examination includes observation (posture, swelling, deformity, gait), active and passive range of movement (noting end-feel — e.g. hard bony, firm capsular, empty in acute pathology), resisted isometric tests (contractile tissue), muscle strength (Oxford scale 0–5), neurological examination (dermatomes, myotomes, reflexes, neural tension tests such as straight leg raise and slump), palpation, accessory joint movements (Maitland grades I–V), and special tests (e.g. Lachman for ACL, McMurray for meniscus, Neer and Hawkins–Kennedy for shoulder impingement). Outcome measures such as the visual analogue or numeric pain rating scale, Oswestry Disability Index, and goniometry quantify progress.

topics.title: Spinal Conditions
topics.summary: Low back pain, disc prolapse, neck pain, spondylosis and management principles.

material.heading: Low back pain
material.body: Low back pain is among the leading causes of disability worldwide and in Nigeria, common among farmers, traders, drivers and health workers. Most (about 90%) is non-specific mechanical back pain. Specific causes include lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy (commonly L4/5 and L5/S1 — dermatomal leg pain, positive SLR, altered reflexes), spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication relieved by flexion), spondylolisthesis, and serious pathology (spinal TB — Pott's disease, metastases, fractures, cauda equina). Management of non-specific pain: reassurance and education, advice to stay active, exercise therapy (motor control, strengthening, general exercise), manual therapy as an adjunct, and cognitive functional approaches; bed rest is discouraged. The McKenzie approach classifies patients by directional preference and centralisation of symptoms.

material.heading: Neck and spondylosis
material.body: Neck pain is often associated with posture, prolonged phone and computer use, and whiplash injuries. Cervical spondylosis (degenerative change) may cause radiculopathy (commonly C6 and C7) or myelopathy (spinal cord compression — clumsy hands, gait disturbance, upper motor neuron signs; needs surgical referral). Management includes education, postural correction, deep neck flexor and scapular strengthening, mobilisation and manipulation (with screening for vertebrobasilar insufficiency and upper cervical instability), and ergonomic advice. Ankylosing spondylitis (inflammatory back pain in young men, morning stiffness > 30 minutes improving with exercise; HLA-B27) requires exercise to maintain posture and chest expansion alongside medical treatment.

topics.title: Upper Limb Conditions
topics.summary: Shoulder pain, frozen shoulder, tennis elbow, carpal tunnel and hand rehabilitation.

material.heading: Shoulder
material.body: Subacromial pain (impingement or rotator cuff tendinopathy) causes a painful arc (60–120° abduction) and pain on resisted movements; management centres on progressive rotator cuff and scapular strengthening. Rotator cuff tears (supraspinatus most often) cause weakness; large tears in younger patients may need repair. Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder — common in diabetics) passes through painful freezing, frozen (stiff) and thawing phases over 1–3 years, with the capsular pattern: loss of external rotation > abduction > internal rotation; treatment includes pain relief, gentle mobilisation, stretching and sometimes steroid injection or hydrodilatation. Anterior shoulder dislocation is the commonest dislocation; rehabilitation restores stability through strengthening.
keyPoints: Frozen shoulder: external rotation lost most

material.heading: Elbow, wrist and hand
material.body: Lateral epicondylalgia (tennis elbow) involves the common extensor origin (extensor carpi radialis brevis) — pain with gripping and resisted wrist extension; managed with load management, progressive (eccentric/isometric) loading, and counterforce braces. Medial epicondylalgia (golfer's elbow) affects the flexor origin. Carpal tunnel syndrome is median nerve compression at the wrist — numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers, worse at night; positive Phalen's and Tinel's tests; managed with night splints in neutral, nerve gliding, steroid injection or surgical release. De Quervain's tenosynovitis affects abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis (positive Finkelstein test). Hand therapy after tendon repairs and fractures uses protocols of protected early mobilisation and splinting.
keyPoints: Tennis elbow: ECRB, resisted wrist extension
Carpal tunnel: median nerve, Phalen's and Tinel's

topics.title: Lower Limb and Sports Injuries
topics.summary: Ankle sprains, knee ligament and meniscal injuries, patellofemoral pain and tendinopathy.

material.heading: Acute soft-tissue injury
material.body: Acute soft-tissue injury management has evolved from RICE to PEACE & LOVE: Protect, Elevate, Avoid anti-inflammatories (in the first days), Compress, Educate; then Load, Optimism, Vascularisation (pain-free aerobic exercise) and Exercise. Lateral ankle sprains (usually the anterior talofibular ligament, inversion injury) are the commonest sports injury; the Ottawa ankle rules identify who needs X-ray. Rehabilitation progresses range, strength, proprioception (balance board) and sport-specific drills to reduce recurrence. Hamstring strains are common in sprinters and footballers; eccentric strengthening (Nordic curls) reduces risk.

material.heading: Knee and tendons
material.body: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries occur with non-contact pivoting (pop, rapid swelling — haemarthrosis); management is surgical reconstruction or structured rehabilitation, with return to sport after about 9–12 months and criteria-based testing. Meniscal tears cause joint-line pain, locking and positive McMurray test. Patellofemoral pain (common in young athletes) is managed with hip and quadriceps strengthening and load modification. Tendinopathies (Achilles, patellar) are degenerative, load-related conditions best treated with progressive tendon loading (isometric, eccentric, heavy slow resistance), not rest alone. Injury prevention programmes (e.g. FIFA 11+) reduce injuries in football, Nigeria's most popular sport.

topics.title: Fractures, Joint Replacement and Arthritis
topics.summary: Fracture healing and rehabilitation, total joint replacement, osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.

material.heading: Fractures and arthroplasty
material.body: Bone healing proceeds through haematoma, inflammation, soft callus, hard callus and remodelling (adult long bones unite in about 6–12 weeks, lower limb longer). Physiotherapy during immobilisation maintains the movement and strength of free joints, prevents complications (chest infection, DVT, pressure sores, stiffness) and teaches mobility with walking aids according to weight-bearing status (non, partial, full). Complications include malunion, non-union, compartment syndrome and complex regional pain syndrome. In Nigeria, traditional bone setters treat many fractures, sometimes causing malunion, gangrene or amputation. After total hip replacement (posterior approach), avoid hip flexion > 90°, adduction past midline and internal rotation; after total knee replacement, early range (goal ≥ 90–110° flexion) and quadriceps strengthening are vital.
keyPoints: THR posterior: avoid flexion > 90°, adduction, IR

material.heading: Arthritis
material.body: Osteoarthritis (OA), the commonest arthritis, especially of the knee in older and overweight Nigerians, causes pain on activity, brief morning stiffness (< 30 minutes), crepitus and bony enlargement. Core management: education, exercise (strengthening and aerobic) and weight loss, with walking aids and bracing as adjuncts; joint replacement for end-stage disease. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis of small joints (symmetrical), with prolonged morning stiffness and deformities (ulnar deviation, swan-neck and boutonnière). During flares: rest, splinting and gentle range; in remission: strengthening, aerobic exercise, joint protection and energy conservation advice alongside disease-modifying drugs. Gout (monosodium urate crystals, often first MTP joint) is managed medically.
